Life from age 4 to 16

I like being able to trace what connects to what. Paid learning sounds good to me, but I still want someone qualified to show me what the real work involves before I decide that the classroom version tells the whole story.

  • family: Lives with his mother, stepfather, and younger sibling.
  • finances: Modest stable income; paid learning has practical appeal.
  • geography: Garland, Texas.
  • cultureLanguages: English-speaking household with relatives working in varied occupations.
  • school: Public high school with supervised low-voltage classroom kits.
  • accessOpportunities: School diagrams and adult-guided household measuring; no electrical installation experience.
  • Age 4–5

    In 2014, Ash enjoyed assembling toy tracks and making sure every piece connected before starting a race. He also liked drawing imaginary animals, rarely feeling any need to make their parts fit a believable explanation.

  • Age 6–7

    At six, he began helping a parent measure shelves before buying storage boxes. During 2017, he learned that a small measuring error could matter even when an object looked approximately right from across the room.

  • Age 8–9

    In 2018, Ash joined a school craft group and liked projects with understandable diagrams. He became frustrated by instructions that omitted a step, then learned to compare the picture with the parts before deciding the whole project was impossible.

  • Age 10–11

    During 2020, he completed practical school assignments at home with adult help where needed. He liked having a clear sequence and a partner to ask, but sometimes avoided starting when he was unsure which materials could be used safely.

  • Age 12–13

    At twelve, Ash encountered a low-voltage circuit kit in class. In 2023, he enjoyed following its diagram and tracing a loose connection, finding that a small, carefully checked change restored the behavior the instructions described.

  • Age 14–15

    Across 2024 and 2025, Ash completed supervised kit exercises and helped measure parts for a household project. Paid apprenticeship learning began to sound attractive, while he recognized that actual electrical installation remained entirely unfamiliar and required appropriate training.

  • Age 16

    At sixteen in 2026, Ash is comparing Texas apprenticeship information, technical courses, and possible college study. He wants practical teamwork, a dependable car, and growing savings, without assuming a school kit establishes readiness for independent electrical work.

Conditional plan preview

Conditional preview of the first displayed career, to test preparation and money. This is not a student choice or a correct-career answer key.

Career: Electricians

Preparation: Texas electrician license for non-exempt work.

  • Start with an apprentice license and supervised work.
  • Journeyman: 8,000 supervised hours and exam.
  • Public electrical work runs through a licensed contractor.

Training budget before aid: $2,295 · 1.0 study years in this reference

Still needs funding: $2,295 · loan payments $0/month · included in lifestyle: no

Annual pay before tax: $43,825 · Published paid-training example · apprenticeship

Chosen-life income range: $80,000–$110,000

Budget result: This pay does not cover your lifestyle. Your costs and savings are higher than your take-home pay.

Financial assumptions: Supported wishes: dependable car, growing savings and steady home life. Used-car and stronger saving choices represent these wishes; housing tenure and exact consumption are modest single-adult reference assumptions, not inferred from current income.

Next steps

  • An earlier activity

    I like being able to trace what connects to what. Paid learning sounds good to me, but I still want someone qualified to show me what the real work involves before I decide that the classroom version tells the whole story.

  • Explore electrical work safely

    Visit a public training demonstration or approved student program. Practice algebra, measurement, and reading diagrams. Do not work on live wiring.

  • Compare a paid apprenticeship and college options

    Austin ETA combines four years and 8,000 hours of training. Review admission steps, published pay, tuition, tools, and Texas licensing. Compare technical college classes and construction-management study too.

  • Ask an apprentice and a qualified electrician

    Ask about hours, travel to job sites, physical demands, tuition, and how pay changes with completed training. Ask which pay figures are that employer’s rates and which are area-wide estimates.
